vocab.extendedMeaning: to dream / to have a dream (verb). The noun covers both sleep dreams and ambitions; context decides which one.
patterns: dream of/about + sb/sth - to dream about somebody or something
dream of/about + doing sth - to dream of doing something
dream that + clause - to dream that something happened, or to dream of a future event
daydream about - to let your mind wander, to fantasise

vocab.extendedMeaning: a historical era or period; a very long time (for ages)
patterns: How old is ...? - asking about age
What's ... age? / What age is ...? - two more ways to ask about age
... is <number> years old. / His age is <number>. - answering
at the age of + number / at age + number - at the age of ...
noun + of his/her own age - the same age as him/her
for ages - for a very long time

grammar.point: The core idea of the prepositions of / from / in / on
grammar.coreIdea: of = a link between two things; from = leaving a starting point and setting off; in = inside, within a frame; on = on top of, making contact with a surface
rules: A preposition is not a Chinese word to be memorised but a spatial or logical idea: link (of), starting point (from), container (in), contact surface (on).

Change the preposition and the verb changes meaning: dream of (to hope to do) against dream about (to see in a dream); believe in (to trust, to have faith) against believe sb (to believe what somebody says).

examples.en: He'd been dreaming of her.
examples.gloss: He kept dreaming about her.

examples.en: Listen, I shall be thinking of you always.
examples.gloss: Listen, I will always remember you.

examples.en: She began to walk away from him.
examples.gloss: She started to walk away from him.

examples.en: I don't like to borrow from friends.
examples.gloss: I don't like borrowing money from friends.

examples.gloss: I was stuck in a traffic jam for half an hour.

commonMistakes: Treating a preposition as a Chinese equivalent: from is not only 'from', it carries the movement of leaving a starting point (p8).
on marks a contact surface, so concentrate on and The check is on me both take on, never in (p8).
grammar.reviewNote: Handout note: review of prepositions, New Concept Book 1 L25-L28.

grammar.coreIdea: A verb plus a preposition behaves like a transitive verb, so an object can follow directly
rules: Verb + preposition = a phrasal verb; the whole unit works like one transitive verb.
The object follows the preposition straight away: dream of + doing sth, and note that the verb after a preposition takes -ing.

examples.en: She dreamed of becoming an actress.
examples.gloss: Her ambition was to become an actress.

examples.en: I dreamt about you last night.
examples.gloss: You were in my dream last night.

commonMistakes: After a preposition a verb must take -ing: dreamed of receiving, not dreamed of receive (p4, p8).

grammar.coreIdea: of marks a link, so verb + of means 'connected with something'
rules: consist of - to be made up of
hear of - to hear about, to know of

examples.en: Breakfast consists of bread and milk.
examples.gloss: Breakfast is made up of bread and milk.

examples.en: Have you heard of her?
examples.gloss: Do you know about her?

commonMistakes: consist of is not used in the passive: not 'Breakfast is consisted of ...'. The handout does not expand on this; read the whole unit as a phrasal verb.

grammar.coreIdea: from is the starting point, so verb + from marks a source or a cause
rules: benefit from - to gain from something
suffer from - to be troubled by an illness or pain

examples.en: Many thousands have benefited from the new treatment.
examples.gloss: Tens of thousands of people have gained from the new treatment.

examples.en: She's suffering from back pain.
examples.gloss: She is troubled by back pain.

commonMistakes: receive sth from sb and hear from sb also take from; note the handout's equation receive a letter from = hear from (p4).

grammar.point: Verb + in - in, within a frame
grammar.coreIdea: in is a container or a frame, so verb + in marks being inside a range or a framework
rules: believe in - to trust, to have faith in
fill in - to complete a form

examples.en: My son believes in Santa Claus.
examples.gloss: My son has faith in Father Christmas.

examples.en: Please fill in this application form.
examples.gloss: Please complete this application form.

commonMistakes: believe in sb means to trust or have faith in somebody; believe sb means to believe what somebody says. The handout gives only believe in, so the contrast is a natural extension of the preposition idea.

grammar.point: Verb + on - on, on the surface
grammar.coreIdea: on marks a contact surface, so verb + on means focusing on something
rules: concentrate on - to give all your attention to something

examples.en: Let's call on Kate on the way home.
examples.gloss: Let's visit Kate on our way home.

examples.en: Focus on your own problems.
examples.gloss: Give your attention to your own problems.

examples.en: concentrate on sth
examples.gloss: To give your full attention to something.

commonMistakes: The on of focus on and concentrate on cannot become in or at (p8, p9).

grammar.coreIdea: A few verbs mean the same with or without the preposition; the preposition merely makes the direction explicit
rules: He fought the enemy. = He fought against the enemy.

examples.en: He fought the enemy.
examples.gloss: He fought against the enemy.

examples.en: He fought against the enemy.
examples.gloss: The same meaning with the preposition added.

commonMistakes: Do not treat 'verb + preposition = phrasal verb' as an absolute rule; some verbs mean the same either way (p9).

grammar.coreIdea: In this pattern the noun can take an adjective in front of it, and the preposition stays at the end
rules: pay close attention to - an adjective can be added before the noun

examples.en: Pay attention to what the teacher says.
examples.gloss: Listen carefully to what the teacher says.

examples.en: He paid scant attention to what the teacher said.
examples.gloss: He hardly listened to what the teacher said.

commonMistakes: When an adjective such as close or scant is added before attention, the preposition to is still needed (p10).

text.original: My daughter, Jane, never dreamed of receiving a letter from a girl of her own age in Holland. Last year, we were travelling across the Channel and Jane put a piece of paper with her name and address on it into a bottle. She threw the bottle into the sea. She never thought of it again, but ten months later, she received a letter from a girl in Holland. Both girls write to each other regularly now. However, they have decided to use the post office. Letters will cost a little more, but they will certainly travel faster.
text.gloss: Jane, the writer's daughter, never expected a letter from a girl her own age in Holland. Last year, while crossing the English Channel, she put a piece of paper with her name and address on it into a bottle and threw the bottle into the sea. She forgot about it, but ten months later a letter arrived from a girl in Holland. The two girls now write to each other regularly, yet they have decided to use the post office, which will cost a little more but will certainly be faster.

timeline.event: My daughter, Jane, never dreamed of receiving a letter from a girl of her own age in Holland.
timeline.gloss: Jane never expected a letter from a girl her own age in Holland.
timeline.note: dreamed is past simple: it sets the whole story in the past. never strengthens the negative: 'never at that time'.

timeline.event: we were travelling across the Channel
timeline.gloss: We were crossing the English Channel.
timeline.note: Before 'and' the past continuous describes the background, an action in progress; across stresses moving over a surface.

timeline.event: Jane put a piece of paper with her name and address on it into a bottle
timeline.gloss: Jane put a piece of paper with her name and address on it into a bottle.
timeline.note: After 'and' the past simple carries the point of the sentence, the single finished action: put sth into a bottle.

timeline.event: She threw the bottle into the sea.
timeline.gloss: She tossed the bottle into the sea.
timeline.note: throw sth into - to toss something into something; into stresses 'going in'.

timeline.event: she received a letter from a girl in Holland
timeline.gloss: She got a letter from a girl in Holland.
timeline.note: The point of the sentence sits after 'but': the story is not over. receive sth from sb; in Holland adds where the girl lives.

timeline.event: Both girls write to each other regularly now.
timeline.gloss: The two girls now write to each other at regular intervals.
timeline.note: The time marker is now. Both takes a plural noun and a plural verb; regularly shows how often they write.

timeline.time: Now (done, with an effect on now)
timeline.event: However, they have decided to use the post office.
timeline.gloss: Even so, they have made up their minds to use the post office.
timeline.note: have decided is present perfect and stresses the effect on the present: no more drift bottles. However starts the sentence and is followed by a comma.

timeline.event: Letters will cost a little more, but they will certainly travel faster.
timeline.gloss: Letters will cost slightly more, but they will certainly be faster.
timeline.note: The future simple states what is very likely to happen. cost takes a thing as its subject: sth cost sb + money. a little more and faster are the comparative forms of much and fast.

logic.relation: It joins two complete clauses and carries two tenses: before and, the background action in progress (past continuous); after and, the point of the sentence, the finished action (past simple).
The point is after but: the story is not over.
It marks a contrast and shows that the way they send letters has changed. It starts the sentence and takes a comma.
both refers to Jane and the Dutch girl together; each other means 'one another' - people doing the same thing and feeling the same way.

points.detail: Jane is an appositive to My daughter: it tells us the daughter's name and is set off by commas.

dreamed is past simple because the story happened in the past; dream of doing sth means to dream or hope to do something; never strengthens the negative. never + past simple means 'never at that time' (compare: I never knew you had a twin sister.).
receive a letter from = hear from, to get a letter from somebody (compare: I used to hear from my best friend.).
of one's own age means 'the same age' (compare: She needs more friends of her own age.).

Country and region: The Netherlands and Holland both name the country, but the official name is the Netherlands. The adjective is Dutch (Dutch people, the Dutch language). One person is a Dutchwoman or a Dutchman; the Dutch means the Dutch people as a whole.
a piece of paper - one sheet; paper is uncountable (compare: Write it down on a piece of paper.).

points.target: with her name and address on it
points.detail: with means 'having, carrying'; do not turn the meaning into the verb write just because of the translation.

points.target: She never thought of it again
points.detail: never + past simple means 'never thought of it at that time'; think of means to think about, to recall; it stands for the glass bottle thrown away earlier (compare: I never thought of him again.).

points.target: Both girls write to each other regularly now.
points.detail: The tense changes to the present simple; the time marker is now; both takes a plural noun, so both girls takes a plural verb; regularly shows how often they write; each other means 'one another'.
Present perfect, stressing the effect on the present: they no longer send letters in bottles.

The subject of cost is a thing: sth cost sb + money. more is the comparative of the adverb much; a little more states by how much - slightly more. faster is the comparative of the adverb fast. certainly strengthens the statement and shows the writer agrees with using the post office.

reviews.en: Last year, however, it came into use.
reviews.gloss: Handout note: the airport began to use it last year.

reviews.en: Neither of us spoke during the journey.
reviews.gloss: Neither of the two of us said a word during the journey.

linking.detail: Blue arcs under of and under of receiving: dreamed, of and receiving run together as one chain.
Arcs under girl and under of her; of her is weak and runs on.
Arc under own: own + age, a consonant linking into a vowel.
The t of Last is marked in blue and joins year: /t/ + /j/.
Arcs under name and under and: name + and + address.
Arcs under on and under it: on + it.
The d of and is marked in blue: and is weakened and joins Jane.
Arcs under of and under it: thought + of + it.
Arc under letter: the r of letter joins from.
Arc under cost a, and little carries a separate /flap t/ mark.

specialMarks.detail: Sense-group pause: ... address on it // into a bottle. Break the breath here.
Intrusive sound: a light /w/ is inserted between into and a, so into a bottle is read into-(w)-a bottle.
American flap: the t / tt of letter, bottle and little becomes a flap.
Weak forms and elision: the h of with her name (the /h/ is usually dropped), the d of and, the silent e of write, the -ed of decided. See the images.

stress.detail: /ˈdɔːtər/ - the stress falls on the first syllable, daugh-.
The handout's pronunciation page marks no sentence stress and no intonation; it shows only the transcriptions, linking, flap t, weak forms and pause listed above. Nothing is guessed here.

writing.storyPlan: Story plan in English (the handout gives this plan and then the model text): my best friend Mary never expected an email from a boy her own age. Last year, while we were studying in the library, Mary put a note with her name and email address on it into a book and put the book back on the shelf. She never thought about the book again, but ten months later she got an email from a boy. He must have read the book with the note in it. The two of them now write regularly, and they have decided to meet up one day.
writing.model: My best friend, Mary, never dreamed of receiving an email from a boy of her own age. Last year, we were studying in the library and Mary put a note with her name and email address on it into a book. She put the book back on the shelf. She never thought of it again, but ten months later, she received an email from a boy. The boy must have read the book with that note. They write to each other regularly now. They have decided to meet up one day.
template: 1 Opening (past simple): My best friend, ___ (name), never dreamed of receiving a ___ (object) from a ___ (person) of his/her own age.
2 Background + key action (past continuous + past simple): Last year, we were ___ -ing ___ and ___ (subject) put a ___ (note/object) with his/her name and ___ on it into a ___.
3 Follow-up action (past simple): He/She put the ___ back ___.
4 Turning point + time jump (past simple): He/She never thought of it again, but ___ months later, he/she received a ___ from ___.
5 Deduction (must have done): The ___ must have read/seen the ___ with that ___.
6 Present situation (present simple + now): They write to each other regularly now.
7 Decision (present perfect): They have decided to ___ one day.
usefulPatterns: never dreamed of receiving ... from a ... of his/her own age - never expected to get something from somebody the same age
we were travelling/studying ... and ... put ... into ... - past continuous sets the background, past simple delivers the point
with his/her name and address on it - carrying his or her name and address
never thought of it again, but ten months later ... - forgot all about it, yet ten months later ...
must have read the book with that note - certainly read the book containing the note
have decided to use/meet up - present perfect for a decision already made
cost a little more, but ... travel faster - a little dearer, but much quicker
writing.notes: The model text matches the handout's English model. The handout prints only the story plan plus the model; the seven template steps are the model's own structure broken down.

order.target: Jane put a piece of paper into a bottle.
She threw the bottle into the sea.

order.hint: Present perfect; However takes a comma.

write.intro: Write the imitation one sentence at a time. The names and places are already given; you only build the key chunks. Click a word chip or type your own, then check that sentence.
write.modelNote: The handout's own model text is the answer key for the seven frames.

frames.label: Sentence 1 - opening (past simple)

blanks.hint: a person of the same age

frames.model: My best friend, Mary, never dreamed of receiving an email from a boy of her own age.

frames.label: Sentence 2 - background + key action (past continuous + past simple)

blanks.hint: your friend's name (given already if you like)

frames.model: Last year, we were studying in the library and Mary put a note with her name and email address on it into a book.

frames.label: Sentence 3 - follow-up action (past simple)

blanks.hint: the same object as in sentence 2

frames.model: She put the book back on the shelf.

frames.label: Sentence 4 - turning point and time jump (past simple)

parts.t: She never thought of it again, but

frames.model: She never thought of it again, but ten months later, she received an email from a boy.

frames.label: Sentence 5 - deduction (must have done)
frames.model: The boy must have read the book with that note.

frames.label: Sentence 6 - now and the decision (present simple + present perfect)
frames.model: They write to each other regularly now. They have decided to meet up one day.

frames.label: Sentence 7 - your own ending (free writing)
frames.prompt: Write the last sentence yourself. What will happen next? Use will.
frames.model: They will meet in the library next year, and they will certainly become good friends.

practiceNote: 45 interactive items: 9 multiple choice, 12 gap fills, 9 true/false, 6 word-order tasks, 3 matching tasks and 7 guided writing frames (the last frame is free writing). Every item gives instant feedback and the reason; all content comes from the handout p1-p10.
